newsitem.title: USA: Harvard to pay U.S. $775,000 over thefts of drugs.
newsitem.headline: Harvard to pay U.S. $775,000 over thefts of drugs.

text.p: Harvard University agreed on Monday to pay $775,000 to settle all claims stemming from drug thefts and sloppy record keeping at its pharmacy, U.S. Attorney Donald Stern said.
The university operates a pharmacy in Harvard Square in Cambridge, Massachusetts, where its students, faculty members and administrators can have prescriptions filled.

"We allege that Harvard fell considerably short of its legal requirements in several areas," Stern said. "The upshot was thefts of drugs, inaccurate inventories, sloppy storage and improper distribution of drugs to unregistered sites."
Stern said he considered the problems "to be significant missteps by Harvard." "They recognised the fault and are now paying a record fine," he said.

Harvard noticed the thefts of controlled substances, including cough syrup with codeine, and a number of anti-anxiety drugs such as lorazepam, oxazepam and temazepam, and notified the Drug Enforcement Administration in November 1995.
A pharmacy technician was subsequently accused of the thefts, and Stern's office said the technician was now facing state drug charges.
"But the fact remains that there were significant and persistent violations, and they're now required to pay about three-quarters of a million dollars to settle those claims," Stern said.
Stern said the federal fine was the largest ever paid in Massachusetts. He added that Harvard had admitted no guilt and had denied that it violated any laws.
Harvard University spokesman James Rowe said in a telephone interview that "no patient was ever harmed."

The university agreed "to settle this because of the very complex regulatory scheme," he said, referring to federal allegations that Harvard had shipped anti-anxiety drugs to its business, medical and law schools without properly recording the transfers.
"We have decided to resolve this civil matter in a way that will avoid very expensive and time-consuming litigation," he said.
